newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. heart man due in Moscow, Yeltsin "optimistic".
newsitem.headline: U.S. heart man due in Moscow, Yeltsin "optimistic".

text.p: U.S. heart surgery pioneer Michael Debakey returns to Moscow on Sunday to advise doctors preparing to operate on President Boris Yeltsin, said by his wife to have "optimism in his eyes" about his imminent operation.
Yeltsin's wife Naina, in a television interview, also said her husband was cracking jokes with his doctors.

Speaking to ORT television at the Barvikha sanatorium where Yeltsin is preparing for a bypass operation, she said the rest of the family were more nervous than Yeltsin himself. "Of course he is worried, but he is outwardly calm."
"He has a good contact with his doctors. I hear humour and jokes," she said, adding that Yeltsin was receiving lots of letters of support and many people were suggesting folk remedies.
"He has optimism in his eyes. As always when he has decided something he believes it will turn out all right," she added.

But she said the family were keeping from him news reports "which we think he should not see". She gave as an example newspaper attacks on his daughter Tatyana which have accused her of bringing documents for her father to sign.
DeBakey, 88, who was due to arrive in Moscow on Sunday afternoon, said Yeltsin had been treated for anaemia and thyroid problems and that he appeared now to be ready for surgery.
He examined Yeltsin in late September and predicted a full recovery for the president, but recommended that he rest for at least six weeks before the operation.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the Western leader closest to Yeltsin, made a brief stopover in Moscow on Saturday for talks with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and passed on his good wishes.
"In these coming days we wish Boris Yeltsin all the best," Kohl told journalists after meeting Chernomyrdin for an hour at Vnukovo airport.

"I hope the president will return (to work) soon and refreshed," Kohl said. He indicated no major decision on NATO enlargement -- a sore point for Moscow -- would be taken until the Russian president was back in action.

Chernomyrdin, who will stand in for Yeltsin during the operation, received personal praise from Kohl, who said: "These are by no means easy times and it is important that you are here to act with a sense of duty and responsibility."
The health of the 65-year-old president is a subject of serious concern for Western government and for investors worried about political stability.
Yeltsin's illness has been accompanied by infighting in Moscow and charges from the opposition that the country is being run in his name by his chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.
But Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, in a radio interview on Saturday, stressed that Yeltsin was personally studying and signing all the decrees issued over his signature.
